title: APIs and REST as a contract
story:
Two organisations integrating across a network have a problem that is not technical: the party on the other side cannot be upgraded on your schedule. Every bespoke arrangement between you becomes a permanent obligation, because breaking it requires coordinating a change with people who have their own priorities. The value of an architectural style here is that it makes the obligations small and known in advance.

Fielding derives the style in chapter 5 of his 2000 dissertation, and the derivation matters more than the result. He starts from a system with no constraints at all and adds them one at a time, saying what each buys. Client-server separates the user interface from data storage so the components can evolve independently. Statelessness keeps session state entirely on the client. Cacheability requires responses to declare whether they may be stored. A layered system means a client cannot ordinarily tell whether it is connected to the end server or to an intermediary along the way. Code on demand is optional.

Then the one he calls fundamental to the design of any such system: the uniform interface, defined by four sub-constraints. Identification of resources. Manipulation of resources through representations. Self-descriptive messages. And hypermedia as the engine of application state. His stated purpose for it is that it simplifies and decouples the architecture, enabling each part to evolve independently — which is the same goal as the whole exercise, applied to the interface itself.

The fourth sub-constraint is the one almost nobody implements, and saying so is the honest version of this lesson. Hypermedia as the engine of application state means the responses tell the client what it can do next, by including the links, so the client does not need to have the set of valid transitions compiled into it. Virtually every interface described as conforming to this style instead publishes a document of URL templates that clients hard-code. That is a perfectly reasonable design. It is not this one, and the property it forfeits is precisely the one the constraint existed to provide: the ability to change the transitions without changing every client.

Which gives the point to carry. The constraints are what produce the benefits, so an interface that adopts the vocabulary and drops the constraints keeps the label and loses the properties. If your clients hard-code paths, your paths are a contract and you will be maintaining them for as long as the clients exist — and that is a decision worth making deliberately rather than discovering later.

problem.name: Constraint-derived interface style
problem.shape: Two independently governed systems must integrate, and neither can be changed on the other's schedule.
tell: clients hard-code paths and construct them from templates
an interface is called RESTful and returns no links
a change requires coordinating with every consumer
state about a conversation is held on the server between requests
problem.move: Decide which constraints you are actually adopting and which you are not, and be explicit about it. If clients hard-code paths, treat those paths as a versioned contract with the maintenance obligation that implies. If you want to change transitions freely, you have to put the links in the responses and make clients follow them.
problem.invariant: The properties of the style come from the constraints rather than from the vocabulary. Adopting the verbs without the constraints yields the name and not the benefits.
problem.breaks: The full style is more expensive for the common case. Clients driven by links are harder to write, harder to test and harder to debug than clients that know their URLs, so the constraint that buys evolvability is the one most often dropped — usually correctly, and almost always without anyone recording that the trade was made.

cost.time: self-descriptive messages carry more per exchange, and link-driven clients take more exchanges to discover what they can do
cost.space: representations larger than a bespoke payload, since they describe themselves
cost.beats: a bespoke protocol, which is smaller and forfeits caches, proxies and tooling, and which makes every change a coordinated release with every consumer

worked.problem: Which constraint of this architectural style does almost nobody implement, and what does dropping it cost?
worked.reasoning:
Hypermedia as the engine of application state — the fourth sub-constraint of the uniform interface — and what it costs is the ability to change your interface without changing every client.

The constraint says the responses carry the links describing what the client may do next, so the client discovers valid transitions at runtime rather than having them compiled in. A client starts at one known entry point and navigates from there, following what it is given.

What almost every interface described this way does instead is publish documentation of URL templates, which clients construct paths from and hard-code. This is worth being clear about: it is a reasonable engineering decision and usually the right one. It is simply not this constraint, and the difference is not cosmetic.

The cost is specific. Because the transitions live in the clients rather than in the responses, every path you expose is now a contract. Change a path and you break consumers. Restructure a resource and you coordinate a release with every team that integrates with you. That is the exact obligation the constraint existed to remove, which is why the derivation puts it under the uniform interface, whose stated purpose is to simplify and decouple the architecture so each part can evolve independently.

I would also explain why it is dropped so consistently, because the reason is legitimate. Link-driven clients are harder to write, harder to test and much harder to debug — a failure becomes a question about what the server offered rather than about what the client requested, and the tooling for that is poor. Meanwhile hard-coded paths are obvious, debuggable and trivial to mock. For an interface with a handful of known consumers inside one organisation, coordinating a change is cheap and the constraint buys little.

So my answer is that the constraint is usually dropped correctly and almost never recorded as a decision. What I would want on a design is the acknowledgement: we are publishing paths as a contract, we will version them, and the cost of changing them is a coordinated release with every consumer. That converts a silent obligation into a known one.

And the general point behind it, which generalises past this style: the properties come from the constraints, not from the vocabulary. An interface that uses the verbs and drops the constraints has the name and not the benefits.

problem.practice: Take an interface you maintain and check whether any response contains a link a client is expected to follow. Then list the paths your consumers hard-code, and treat that list as what it is — the contract you have actually committed to.

beats.broke: Two organisations must integrate across a network and every bespoke arrangement becomes a permanent obligation, because the party on the other side cannot be upgraded on your schedule.
beats.fix: Agree on a small set of constraints instead of a bespoke protocol — addressable resources, a uniform set of operations, self-describing messages, and state held by the caller — so intermediaries work and both sides can change independently.
beats.cost: The constraints are what deliver the benefits, so an interface that keeps the vocabulary and drops the constraints keeps the label and loses the properties it was named for.

interview.q: Which constraint of this architectural style does almost nobody implement, and what does dropping it cost?
interview.trap: Treating the omission as a failure to be corrected. It is usually the right engineering decision — link-driven clients are genuinely harder to build and debug — and the actual problem is that the trade is almost never recorded, so the resulting contract obligation arrives as a surprise.
